Consult Summary:
- 51-year-old female with 6 days of dysuria, malodorous urine, suprapubic intermittent pain (7/10) and visible spotting of blood; clinician treated empirically for suspected acute uncomplicated cystitis with a 3-day course of oral antibiotics (unspecified) and advised conservative measures and safety-netting; DDx supports cystitis as most likely.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Pain on urination (dysuria) for 6 days.
  - Malodorous urine and visible blood described as “spots.”
  - Intermittent lower central abdominal (suprapubic) pain, severity 7/10.
- Timeline/progression:
  - Symptoms began ~6 days before consult; patient reports symptoms are ongoing (no improvement documented).
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - No specific exacerbating factors identified; advised to increase fluid intake as part of management.
- Associated symptoms / systems review:
  - No fever or feeling feverish.
  - No loin/flank pain.
  - Able to pass urine.
  - No vaginal discharge reported.
  - No change in appetite, bowel habit, weight loss.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No prior history of urinary tract infections.
  - No recent sexual activity or other precipitating events reported.
  - No history of trauma, surgery, or known kidney disease.

Past Medical History:
- Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).
- No other medical conditions or prior kidney/urinary problems reported.
- No prior surgeries reported.

Medications:
- Mebeverine 200 mg three times daily (patient-reported).
- Antibiotic prescribed for presumed UTI: oral antibiotic, 3-day course (agent not specified in transcript) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Allergies:
  - Clindamycin.

Social History:
- Lives with friends.
- Occupation: support worker.
- Alcohol: occasional; about one glass of wine per week.
- Tobacco: non-smoker.
- No other substance use reported.

Family History:
- No relevant family medical problems reported.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings: Not recorded.

Investigations:
- No labs, urinalysis, urine culture, imaging, or pregnancy test performed or documented during this visit.
- Clinician recommended patient obtain a thermometer and check temperature at home.

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
- Working diagnosis: Acute uncomplicated cystitis (lower urinary tract infection) — most likely given female sex, 6 days of dysuria, suprapubic pain, malodorous urine and visible hematuria; no systemic features to suggest upper tract involvement.

DDx Integration (brief):
- 1) Acute uncomplicated cystitis — supporting: dysuria, suprapubic pain, malodorous urine, visible hematuria; opposing: no urine dip/culture confirmation documented.  
- 2) Urethritis / STI (e.g., Chlamydia, Gonorrhea) — supporting: dysuria and urethral bleeding possible; opposing: patient denied recent sexual activity, no discharge reported.  
- 3) Urolithiasis (bladder/ureteric stone) — supporting: intermittent severe lower abdominal pain and hematuria; opposing: no flank/loin pain or prior stone history.  
- (DDx from provided reasoning is consistent with the transcript; no conflict noted.)

Issue 1: Suspected acute uncomplicated cystitis
- Assessment:
  - Clinical diagnosis based on typical symptoms (dysuria, suprapubic pain, malodorous urine, visible hematuria) in an otherwise well patient without systemic features.
- Plan:
  - Empiric oral antibiotic prescribed for 3 days — antibiotic agent not specified in transcript; dose/route/frequency not documented. (Prescription sent to Knightsbridge Practice pharmacy per patient request.)
  - Advise to start antibiotics as soon as obtained.
  - Increase oral fluids (advised 2.5–3.0 L/day).
  - Optional supportive measures advised: cranberry juice and over-the-counter sachets to alter urine acidity (patient given information will be documented).
  - Advise to obtain a thermometer and monitor temperature.
  - Safety-net instructions: return or seek urgent care if symptoms worsen, develop fever, develop new/worsening loin/flank pain, cannot pass urine, or if symptoms do not improve or recur.

Issue 2: Hematuria (visible spotting)
- Assessment:
  - Most likely secondary to lower urinary tract inflammation/infection given presentation; other causes (stone, urethritis, less likely malignancy) remain in differential if hematuria persists.
- Plan:
  - If visible hematuria persists after treatment, recurs, or other red flags develop, arrange urinalysis/urine microscopy and urine culture and further evaluation (including consideration of STI testing, imaging or urology referral as indicated). (No tests were ordered at this visit per transcript.)

Issue 3: Consideration of alternative/complicating diagnoses (urethritis/STI, urolithiasis, ascending infection)
- Assessment:
  - Urethritis/STI: possible if symptoms persist or do not respond to empiric therapy; sexual history not fully explored.
  - Urolithiasis: possible explanation for hematuria and intermittent severe pain though flank pain absent.
  - Acute pyelonephritis: currently unlikely (no fever/flank pain) but must be considered if clinical course worsens.
- Plan:
  - If symptoms do not improve with initial antibiotic course, or if red flags arise, clinician to pursue further testing (urine culture, STI screening, imaging) and consider alternate/adjunctive treatments or referral.
  - Document allergy to clindamycin to avoid contraindicated agents.

General plan items:
- Prescription sent to Knightsbridge Practice pharmacy; patient advised pickup in ~1 hour to several hours.
- Follow-up only required if not improving, worsening, recurrent symptoms, or red-flag signs as above.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs (temperature not recorded), pregnancy status not documented, no urinalysis/urine dip or culture performed, antibiotic agent/dose/route/frequency not specified in transcript.
- Conflicts: No direct conflicts between transcript and DDx; DDx conclusions are consistent with the clinical history.
- Transcript quality: Audio transcript legible; occasional brief clarification needed but overall adequate for documentation.
